title: Integration, variation, and symmetry
one_line_summary: Finishes the book's mathematical toolkit: tensor densities, the alternating symbol and the metric determinant are used to build invariant integrals and a covariant divergence theorem; the Euler-Lagrange equations are derived and turned into a fast recipe for geodesics and Christoffel symbols; and continuous symmetries of a metric are captured by Killing's equation.
role_in_book: Third and last of the pure-mathematics chapters (Chapter 5 tensor algebra, Chapter 6 tensor calculus, Chapter 7) that separate the special-relativity part from the principles of general relativity. It supplies three tools the physics chapters use constantly: the invariant volume element sqrt(-g) d^4x with the covariant divergence theorem (needed for conservation laws and for the action-based derivation of the field equations in Chapter 11); the variational method with the Lagrangian K = (1/2) g_ab xdot^a xdot^b (reused for free-particle mechanics in Chapter 8 and for Schwarzschild orbits, light bending and perihelion advance in Chapters 16-17); and Killing vectors (used to define stationary and spherically symmetric space-times in Chapter 15, adapted coordinates for black holes in Chapter 17, and plane, cylindrical and axisymmetric gravitational waves in Chapters 22-23).

assumed_background.topic: Transformation laws of contravariant, covariant and mixed tensors; Jacobian of a coordinate change
Parametric description of curves, surfaces and m-dimensional subspaces of a manifold
Lie bracket of vector fields and the Jacobi identity (used in Exercise 7.13)
Lie derivative and the idea of dragging a tensor along a vector field
Affine connection, covariant derivative of tensors, affine geodesics and affine parameters
Metric, index raising and lowering, metric geodesics, Christoffel symbols of both kinds
Metric connection: vanishing covariant derivative of the metric and the formula for partial derivatives of g_ab in terms of Gamma
Riemann tensor and its cyclic identity (for Exercises 7.14-7.15)
Determinants, cofactor expansion along a row, inverse matrix as transposed cofactors over the determinant
Multiple integrals, change of variables with a Jacobian, Green/Gauss/Stokes theorems in R^n
Taylor expansion to first order and integration by parts
Lagrangian mechanics and the principle of least action (helpful context, not strictly required)

learning_objectives: Reader can state the transformation law of a tensor density of weight W and find the weight of products, determinants, g and sqrt(-g).
Reader can write the covariant derivative of a tensor density using the book's -W Gamma^d_{dc} convention and show that a weight +1 vector density has a connection-free divergence.
Reader can express the determinant of a rank-2 tensor with alternating symbols and apply the contractions of epsilon^{abcd} epsilon_{efgh} into generalized Kronecker deltas.
Reader can derive d_c g = g g^{ab} d_c g_ab from cofactor expansion and deduce Gamma^a_{ac} = d_c ln sqrt(-g), nabla_c g = 0 and nabla_c sqrt(-g) = 0.
Reader can explain why d^4x alone is not an invariant measure and write an invariant integral of a scalar field using sqrt(-g).
Reader can state Stokes' theorem for parametrized subspaces and specialize it to Gauss's theorem for densities and to the covariant divergence theorem in four dimensions.
Reader can prove the fundamental lemma of the calculus of variations and derive the Euler-Lagrange equations for one variable, several variables, and fields on a manifold.
Reader can derive the geodesic equation by making the interval stationary, explain the parametrization term (sddot/sdot) xdot^a, and say which parameters are affine.
Reader can apply the K-Lagrangian with 2K = 0, +1 or -1 to write geodesic equations for null, timelike and spacelike curves and read off Christoffel symbols from them.
Reader can distinguish the active push-forward and pull-back maps from passive coordinate changes and define symmetries and isometries of tensor fields.
Reader can derive Killing's equation from a first-order expansion of the isometry condition and find the Killing vectors of simple metrics such as flat Euclidean 3-space.

teaching_approach.summary: A compact, formula-dense toolkit chapter in the component language of Chapters 5-6. Each tool opens with a one-line motivating observation (scalars at separate points can be summed, so integration ought to be possible; a metric left unchanged by a map encodes a symmetry) and is then developed by explicit index manipulation, with frequent '(check)' and '(exercise)' gaps left to the reader. Cheap proofs are given in full (the cofactor route to the derivative of a determinant, the bump-function lemma, the first-order expansion that produces Killing's equation), while standard or messy results are quoted (Stokes' theorem, the null-geodesic variational argument, building finite symmetries from infinitesimal ones). Every thread ends in a working recipe that later physics chapters reuse: sqrt(-g) d^4x, the K-Lagrangian, Killing's equation.
narrative_arc: Generalize tensors to densities by allowing an extra power of the Jacobian, fix a convention for their covariant derivative, and extract the payoff that the divergence of a weight +1 vector density needs no connection.

Introduce the alternating symbol as a weight +1 density, use it to write determinants (so a covariant rank-2 determinant has weight +2), and list the epsilon-epsilon contraction identities in terms of generalized Kronecker deltas.

Apply this to the metric: g has weight +2 and sqrt(-g) weight +1; digress to differentiate an arbitrary determinant through cofactors, express d_c g through Gamma, and conclude that g and sqrt(-g) are covariantly constant.

Motivate integration from the additivity of scalars at different points, observe that the coordinate volume element is a weight -1 density, define parametrized volume elements, state Stokes' theorem, specialize to Gauss's theorem and then to the covariant divergence theorem.

Change subject to the calculus of variations: define functionals and the action, prove the fundamental lemma, derive and repackage the Euler-Lagrange equation, and generalize to many variables and to fields with a Lagrangian density.

Apply the method to the interval to recover the geodesic equation with a parametrization term, identify affine parameters, note the null case, and replace L by K = (1/2) g xdot xdot as the practical recipe that also yields the connection.

Turn to symmetry: diffeomorphisms, push-forward and pull-back, symmetry of a tensor field, isometry; linearize the isometry condition to get Killing's equation as the vanishing Lie derivative of the metric and state the generating theorem.
Exercises consolidate each thread and push the symmetry thread further: the six Euclidean Killing vectors, closure under commutators, and curvature identities satisfied by Killing fields.
signature_moves: Weight bookkeeping: each new object is tagged with the power of the Jacobian it acquires, so the invariance of combinations such as Phi dOmega or sqrt(-g) d^4x is read off by adding weights to zero.
The density covariant derivative convention is chosen so that epsilon, g and sqrt(-g) all have vanishing covariant derivative, and those facts are then presented as confirmations of the convention.
A self-contained linear-algebra digression (derivative of a determinant via cofactors) is inserted exactly where the metric computation needs it.
The fundamental lemma is proved with an explicit (x - xi_1)^4 (x - xi_2)^4 bump rather than by appeal to distribution theory.
The geodesic equation is first derived from the square-root Lagrangian to expose the parametrization term, and only afterwards is the squared Lagrangian K advocated as the efficient method.

Killing's equation is obtained by brute-force Taylor expansion of the finite isometry condition, and the first-order bracket is recognized as the Chapter 6 Lie derivative ('the metric is dragged into itself').

Major results the main text does not develop (six Killing vectors of flat space, closure of Killing vectors under commutators, second derivatives of Killing vectors given by curvature) are carried by hinted exercises.

sections.title: Tensor densities
sections.summary: Defines a tensor density of weight W by a tensor-like transformation law multiplied by J^W, with J the Jacobian of old with respect to new coordinates. Notes that weights add under products, adopts (with an admission of arbitrariness) a covariant derivative carrying an extra -W Gamma^d_{dc} term, writes the vector-density case, and shows that for weight +1 the covariant and ordinary divergences coincide.
concepts: covariant derivative of a tensor density
divergence of a weight +1 vector density
key_moves: Transformation law (7.1): ordinary tensor factors times J^W with J = |dx^a/dx'^b|.
Product rule for weights follows at once from (7.1).
Definition (7.2): usual connection terms minus W Gamma^d_{dc} times the density.
Contracting c with a for W = +1 makes the Gamma^a_{ba} T^b term cancel the -Gamma^b_{ba} T^a term, giving (7.3).

sections.title: The Levi-Civita alternating symbol
sections.summary: Introduces epsilon^{abcd} with components +1, -1, 0 in every chart according to permutation parity, identifies it as a weight +1 contravariant density, uses it to define the determinant of a covariant rank-2 tensor (weight +2), introduces the lower-index weight -1 symbol for contravariant determinants (weight -2), states that both symbols are covariantly constant under (7.2), and defines generalized Kronecker deltas together with the four-dimensional epsilon-epsilon contraction identities.
concepts: determinant of a rank-2 tensor via alternating symbols
key_moves: Index range switched to 0-3, sample component values listed to fix the permutation rule.
Determinant formula (7.4) with 1/4! and two epsilons; weight +2 checked against det T' = J^2 det T.
Covariant constancy of both epsilons (left as Exercise 7.2) offered as a motivation for the density derivative convention.
Generalized deltas written as determinants of ordinary deltas; successive contractions of epsilon^{abcd} epsilon_{efgh} produce factors 1, 1, 2, 3!, 4!.

sections.title: The metric determinant
sections.summary: Shows from the metric transformation law that g is a weight +2 scalar density and, since g < 0 for Lorentzian metrics, that sqrt(-g) is a weight +1 density, so sqrt(-g) times any tensor is a weight +1 density with the divergence property (7.6). A general digression differentiates a determinant through its cofactors, giving d_c g = g g^{ab} d_c g_ab; combining with the metric-connection formula yields d_c g = 2 g Gamma^a_{ac}, hence nabla_c g = 0 and nabla_c sqrt(-g) = 0, so sqrt(-g) passes through covariant derivatives.
concepts: square root of minus the metric determinant
covariant constancy of g and sqrt(-g)
key_moves: Take determinants of (7.5) to get g' = J^2 g, rewrite with -g for negative-signature metrics, take square roots.
Row expansion a = sum_j a_ij A^ij shows the partial derivative of the determinant with respect to an entry is its cofactor (7.8).
Chain rule plus inverse = transposed cofactors / determinant gives d_k a = a b^{ji} d_k a_ij, specialized to (7.9) for symmetric g_ab.
Substituting (6.77) and contracting with g^{ab} collapses to 2 g Gamma^a_{ac} (7.10).
Weight +2 and +1 versions of (7.2) then give (7.11) and (7.12), and the product rule gives (7.13).

sections.title: Integrals and Stokes' theorem
sections.summary: Argues that scalars evaluated at different points can be added, but the coordinate volume element is a weight -1 density, so the natural integrand is a weight +1 scalar density. Defines the tensorial volume element of an m-dimensional parametrized subspace through a generalized Kronecker delta, states Stokes' theorem relating an integral over a region to one over its boundary, specializes to Gauss's theorem for a weight +1 vector density in four dimensions with hypersurface element dS_a and volume element dOmega, and, taking the density to be sqrt(-g) T^a, obtains the covariant divergence theorem.
concepts: additivity of scalars at different points
volume element as a scalar density of weight -1
volume element of an m-dimensional subspace
Gauss's divergence theorem for vector densities
key_moves: (7.14): a sum of scalar values at two points is invariant, suggesting integration is meaningful for the right integrand.
(7.16): antisymmetrized product of tangent vectors dx/du^i times parameter increments gives an m-th rank contravariant tensor element that is also parameter-invariant.
(7.18) stated without proof and identified with the ordinary Stokes theorem in parameter space.
dS_a and dOmega defined by contracting dtau with the weight -1 epsilon_{abcd}; in coordinate parameters dOmega = d^4x, a weight -1 density.
(7.6) and (7.13) convert the partial divergence of sqrt(-g) T^a into sqrt(-g) nabla_a T^a, giving (7.24).

sections.title: The Euler-Lagrange equations
sections.summary: Presented as a digression for completeness. Defines functionals and the action integral of a Lagrangian L(y, y', x), proves the fundamental lemma using a localized fourth-power bump, introduces the variation delta y = epsilon eta with fixed endpoints, shows delta and d/dx commute, expands the action to first order, integrates by parts, and obtains the Euler-Lagrange equation. Introduces the variational derivative and the principle of stationary action, then generalizes to n dependent variables and to m fields on an n-dimensional manifold with a weight +1 Lagrangian density, whose Euler-Lagrange equations are the field equations of a theory.
concepts: fundamental lemma of the calculus of variations
Euler-Lagrange equations for several dependent variables
field equations from a variational principle
key_moves: Lemma proof by contradiction: if phi(xi) > 0, choose eta supported where phi > 0 so the integral is strictly positive.
Variation delta y = epsilon eta(x) vanishing at x_1, x_2; delta(y') = (delta y)'.
First-order Taylor expansion of I[y + delta y], integration by parts, boundary term killed by eta(x_i) = 0, giving (7.28).
Lemma turns delta I = 0 for all eta into (7.29); rewritten compactly as delta L / delta y = 0 (7.30)-(7.32).
Generalization to (7.34) for n functions and (7.36) for fields with commas denoting partial derivatives.

sections.title: The variational method for geodesics
sections.summary: Takes L = (g_ab xdot^a xdot^b)^{1/2} along a timelike curve so that the action is the interval, defines the metric geodesic as the curve of stationary interval with fixed endpoints, and works through the Euler-Lagrange equations. Multiplying by -2L and trading L for L^2 separates a left side that produces g_ab xddot^b plus Christoffel symbols of the first kind from a right side proportional to the rate of change of ds/du, giving the geodesic equation with a parametrization term that vanishes exactly when u is proportional to proper interval (an affine parameter). The spacelike case is left as an exercise.
concepts: metric geodesic as a curve of stationary interval
Christoffel symbols of the first kind
key_moves: Action (7.38) equals the interval s between the endpoints by (6.60).
Three practical difficulties flagged: square roots, parameter freedom, null versus non-null curves.
Rewrite (7.40) as (7.41): d/du(dL^2/dxdot) - dL^2/dx = 2 (dL/dxdot)(dL/du).
Left side evaluates to 2 g_ab xddot^b + 2 {bc,a} xdot^b xdot^c; right side to 2 (sddot/sdot) g_ab xdot^b; raising with g^{ad} gives (7.42).
Setting u = s kills the right side (7.43); affine parameters are those related to s by s-bar = alpha s + beta (7.44).

sections.title: Null geodesics and the K-Lagrangian recipe (end of §7.6)
sections.summary: Notes that L vanishes on null curves so the square-root argument fails, quotes without proof the null geodesic equation with a lambda(u) xdot^a term and the null tangent condition, and defines affine parameters for null geodesics. Summarizes with the recommended method: with an affine parameter, the Euler-Lagrange equations of K = (1/2) g_ab xdot^a xdot^b give the geodesic equations for all three causal types, K is constant with 2K = 0, +1, -1, and Christoffel symbols can be read directly from the resulting equations.
concepts: reading off Christoffel symbols from geodesic equations
key_moves: Null case: L = 0 invalidates division by L; result quoted as xddot + Gamma xdot xdot = lambda(u) xdot with g xdot xdot = 0.
Affine null parameters defined by lambda = 0 and related by u-bar = alpha u + beta (7.45).
Recipe (7.46)-(7.48): Euler-Lagrange equations of K with affine u; proof left as Exercise 7.7.
Comparing the resulting equations with (7.43) lets one read off Gamma^a_{bc} efficiently.

sections.title: Isometries
sections.summary: Motivates symmetries as transformations leaving a metric unchanged, separating discrete from continuous ones. Defines a diffeomorphism acting actively on points, the push-forward and pull-back of a covariant tensor between the points P and Q, and insists that, despite sharing the Jacobian structure of a coordinate change, these formulas move a tensor to a different point and so are active. A symmetry of a tensor field is a map whose pull-back of the field reproduces the field; for the metric this is an isometry (7.52). Linearizing with x-tilde = x + epsilon X(x) and expanding to first order produces the Lie derivative of the metric, which after replacing partial by covariant derivatives becomes Killing's equation. A boxed theorem states that infinitesimal isometries are generated by Killing vectors, and finite continuous isometries are said to be built from infinitesimal ones.
concepts: infinitesimal transformation generated by a vector field
theorem: Killing vectors generate infinitesimal isometries
generation of finite transformations from infinitesimal ones
key_moves: Active map P -> Q with coordinates x -> x-tilde, invertible and smooth.
(7.49) push-forward and (7.50) pull-back written with the same Jacobian structure as a coordinate change but reinterpreted actively.
Symmetry condition (7.51) and its metric case (7.52) compare the pulled-back field with the original at the same point.
Insert (7.53), expand g_cd(x + epsilon X) by Taylor's theorem, keep order epsilon: the bracket is L_X g_ab from (6.17).
Swap partial for covariant derivatives using (6.74) and (6.58) to get nabla_b X_a + nabla_a X_b = 0 (7.55).

sections.title: Exercises and further reading
sections.summary: Fifteen exercises keyed to sections: density derivatives and the constancy of epsilon, a Jacobian version of the determinant-derivative argument, the four-dimensional divergence theorem, practice Euler-Lagrange equations, the spacelike geodesic and K-Lagrangian argument, geodesics and Christoffel symbols of the general spherically symmetric metric, Killing vectors of a 2D metric and of Euclidean 3-space, closure of Killing vectors under linear combination and commutator, and curvature identities satisfied by Killing vectors. Further reading repeats the Chapter 5 list with ten mathematical and relativity references.
key_moves: Exercise 7.11 hint route: Killing's equation plus index permutation forces all second derivatives of X to vanish, leaving rotations and translations.
Exercise 7.13 uses the operator identity for commutators of Lie derivatives to show Killing vectors close under brackets.
Exercises 7.14-7.15 connect Killing vectors to the Riemann tensor.

concepts.name: tensor density
concepts.definition: An indexed quantity that transforms exactly like a tensor of the same index structure except for an extra overall factor J^W, where J is the determinant of the matrix dx^a/dx'^b (old coordinates differentiated by new) and the number W is the weight. Weight zero gives an ordinary tensor.
concepts.how_introduced: Opens the chapter as a bare generalization of the tensor transformation law, with the justification (determinants, volume elements, Lagrangian densities) arriving in later sections. Denoted by gothic letters.
concepts.notes: The sign of a weight depends on whether J is built from dx/dx' (this book) or dx'/dx (some other texts); with this book's choice sqrt(-g) has weight +1 and d^4x weight -1.

concepts.name: additivity of density weights
aliases: weight of a product of densities
concepts.definition: The product (including contractions) of densities of weights W_1 and W_2 is a density of weight W_1 + W_2, because the Jacobian factors multiply.
concepts.how_introduced: Noted in one sentence as the main way densities combine differently from tensors; used implicitly throughout (e.g. epsilon epsilon T T T T has weight 2, sqrt(-g) T^a has weight 1).

concepts.name: scalar density
concepts.definition: A single-component quantity that changes under a coordinate transformation only by the factor J^W. Examples in the chapter: the determinant of a covariant rank-2 tensor (W = +2), sqrt(-g) (W = +1), the coordinate volume element d^4x (W = -1), and a Lagrangian density (W = +1).
concepts.how_introduced: Appears as the zero-index case of a tensor density and becomes central once integration is discussed: only weight +1 scalar densities can be integrated invariantly against d^4x.

concepts.name: covariant derivative of a tensor density
concepts.definition: For a density of weight W, apply all the connection terms one would use for a tensor with the same indices and then subtract W Gamma^d_{dc} times the density. The result is a density of the same weight with one more covariant index.
concepts.how_introduced: Stated as a definition, with the authors admitting other conventions are possible; justified afterwards by the fact that it makes epsilon, g and sqrt(-g) covariantly constant.
concepts.notes: The minus-W term is what makes the weight +1 divergence connection-free; with a symmetric connection the two Gamma terms cancel on contraction.

concepts.name: divergence of a weight +1 vector density
concepts.definition: If T^a (gothic) is a vector density of weight +1 then its covariant divergence equals its plain partial-derivative divergence, and the result is a weight +1 scalar density.
concepts.how_introduced: Presented as the first payoff of the density derivative convention, with a '(check)' prompt; the scalar-density claim is deferred to Exercise 7.3.
prerequisites: covariant derivative of a tensor density
concepts.notes: Relies on the connection being symmetric in its lower indices so that Gamma^a_{ba} T^b and Gamma^b_{ba} T^a match; the book assumes a symmetric connection from Chapter 6.

concepts.name: Levi-Civita alternating symbol
concepts.definition: The totally antisymmetric four-index symbol whose components equal +1 when the indices are an even permutation of 0123, -1 for an odd permutation and 0 if any index repeats, with these same numbers in every coordinate system. The upper-index version epsilon^{abcd} is then a contravariant tensor density of weight +1 and the lower-index version epsilon_{abcd}, with identical numerical values, has weight -1.
concepts.how_introduced: Presented as a many-index relative of the Kronecker delta that fails to be a genuine tensor and is instead a density; a handful of sample component values (including zeros for repeated indices) fix the parity rule, and the determinant formula (7.4) then exhibits its weight.
concepts.notes: Not related to each other by the metric: lowering all indices of epsilon^{abcd} with g_ab gives g epsilon_{abcd}, which has the opposite sign in Lorentzian signature.

concepts.name: determinant of a rank-2 tensor via alternating symbols
concepts.definition: The determinant of a covariant second-rank tensor equals (1/4!) epsilon^{abcd} epsilon^{efgh} T_ae T_bf T_cg T_dh, which makes it a scalar density of weight +2; the analogous formula with lower-index epsilons gives the determinant of a contravariant tensor as a weight -2 density.
concepts.how_introduced: Used to show that the density character of determinants can be read from weights, and checked against det T' = J^2 det T from the transformation law.

concepts.name: generalized Kronecker delta
concepts.definition: A constant tensor with k upper and k lower indices equal to +1 if the upper indices are distinct and form an even permutation of the lower ones, -1 for an odd permutation, and 0 otherwise; equivalently the determinant of the k-by-k array of ordinary Kronecker deltas.
concepts.how_introduced: Defined explicitly for two index pairs, then by determinant expressions for two and three pairs; used in the epsilon contraction identities and in the volume element of a subspace.

concepts.name: epsilon-delta contraction identities
concepts.definition: In four dimensions the product epsilon^{abcd} epsilon_{efgh} equals the four-index generalized delta, and contracting one, two, three or four index pairs gives the three-index delta, 2 times the two-index delta, 3! times the ordinary delta, and 4! respectively.
concepts.how_introduced: Listed without proof immediately after the generalized deltas.
concepts.notes: Valid for the numerical symbols as defined; if one instead lowers indices with a Lorentzian metric an extra minus sign appears.

concepts.name: metric determinant
concepts.definition: g = det(g_ab), the determinant of the covariant metric components; it transforms as a scalar density of weight +2 and is negative for a Lorentzian metric.
concepts.how_introduced: Obtained by taking determinants of the metric transformation law (7.5).
prerequisites: determinant of a rank-2 tensor via alternating symbols

concepts.name: square root of minus the metric determinant
concepts.definition: sqrt(-g), a positive scalar density of weight +1 on a Lorentzian manifold; multiplying any tensor by it produces a weight +1 density, and it supplies the factor that makes coordinate volume integrals invariant.
concepts.how_introduced: Follows from g' = J^2 g after changing sign for negative-signature metrics and taking square roots; immediately put to work in (7.6).
concepts.notes: In a Riemannian (positive-definite) setting the same role is played by sqrt(g).

concepts.name: derivative of a determinant (Jacobi's formula)
concepts.definition: For a matrix A whose entries depend on coordinates, the partial derivative of det A with respect to an entry is that entry's cofactor, so d_k(det A) = det A times the trace of A^{-1} d_k A. For the metric this reads d_c g = g g^{ab} d_c g_ab.
concepts.how_introduced: A self-declared digression in §7.3: expand the determinant along a fixed row, note the cofactors of that row do not contain its entries, then apply the chain rule and the cofactor formula for the inverse.
concepts.notes: Later reused in Chapter 11 to vary sqrt(-g) with respect to g_ab.

concepts.name: contracted Christoffel symbol identity
concepts.definition: For the metric connection, Gamma^a_{ac} = (1/2g) d_c g = d_c ln sqrt(-g).
concepts.how_introduced: Obtained by feeding the metric-connection expression for d_c g_ab (6.77) into Jacobi's formula.

concepts.name: covariant constancy of g and sqrt(-g)
concepts.definition: With the book's density derivative, both the metric determinant (weight +2) and sqrt(-g) (weight +1) have identically vanishing covariant derivatives, so they can be moved through nabla like metric factors.
concepts.how_introduced: Computed directly from (7.2) and the contracted Christoffel identity; the authors note the result is tied to their chosen convention.
prerequisites: covariant derivative of a tensor density

concepts.name: covariant divergence formula
concepts.definition: For any vector field, the covariant divergence equals (1/sqrt(-g)) d_a(sqrt(-g) T^a), so divergences can be computed with partial derivatives alone.
concepts.how_introduced: Implicit in combining (7.6) with (7.13); written out as a chain of equalities in §7.4 just before the covariant divergence theorem.
prerequisites: divergence of a weight +1 vector density
covariant constancy of g and sqrt(-g)
concepts.notes: The book never isolates this one-line formula, though it is the most-used computational consequence; worth making explicit for learners (e.g. the polar-coordinate divergence).

concepts.name: additivity of scalars at different points
concepts.definition: Values of a scalar field at distinct points are coordinate-independent numbers, so their sum is also invariant; this is what makes a Riemann-sum style integral of a suitable integrand meaningful on a manifold.
concepts.how_introduced: Used as the opening motivation for integration, contrasting scalars with general tensors whose components at different points cannot be meaningfully combined.

concepts.name: volume element as a scalar density of weight -1
concepts.definition: The coordinate volume element dOmega = d^4x = dx^0 dx^1 dx^2 dx^3 is not a scalar: under a change of coordinates it acquires a factor 1/J, i.e. it is a scalar density of weight -1.
concepts.how_introduced: Asserted when motivating integration and later confirmed from its definition as (1/4!) epsilon_{abcd} dtau^{abcd}.

concepts.name: integral of a scalar density
concepts.definition: An integral over an n-dimensional region that is coordinate independent because the integrand Phi is a weight +1 scalar density, whose weight cancels the weight -1 of the volume element.
concepts.how_introduced: Deduced from the additivity of scalars plus the weight of dOmega.
prerequisites: volume element as a scalar density of weight -1

concepts.name: invariant volume element
concepts.definition: The combination sqrt(-g) d^4x, whose weights +1 and -1 cancel so that it is a true scalar; integrating a scalar field against it gives a coordinate-independent result.
concepts.how_introduced: Not given its own name in the text but appears as the measure in the covariant divergence theorem (7.24) and in later action integrals.
prerequisites: square root of minus the metric determinant
volume element as a scalar density of weight -1

concepts.name: volume element of an m-dimensional subspace
concepts.definition: For a subspace x^a(u^1, ..., u^m), the antisymmetrized product of the m tangent vectors dx^a/du^i times du^1...du^m, formed with a generalized Kronecker delta. It is a contravariant rank-m tensor under coordinate changes and invariant under reparametrization, so contracting it with a covariant rank-m tensor gives an integrable scalar.
concepts.how_introduced: Defined abstractly for curves, surfaces and hypersurfaces as the ingredient for Stokes' theorem.
formulas: \mathrm{d}\tau^{a_1\cdots a_m} = \delta^{a_1\cdots a_m}_{b_1\cdots b_m}\frac{\partial x^{b_1}}{\partial u^1}\cdots\frac{\partial x^{b_m}}{\partial u^m}\,\mathrm{d}u^1\cdots\mathrm{d}u^m

concepts.name: generalized Stokes' theorem
concepts.definition: The integral of a covariant rank-(m-1) tensor over the boundary of an m-dimensional region equals the integral over the region of its partial derivative contracted with the m-dimensional volume element; in parameter space it reduces to the familiar Stokes theorem in R^n.
concepts.how_introduced: Stated without proof for a simply connected region, then specialized to four dimensions.
prerequisites: volume element of an m-dimensional subspace
concepts.notes: Orientation of the boundary is not discussed; the relative ordering of the derivative index fixes a sign convention (see gaps). In form language this is the integral of d(omega) over Omega equals that of omega over the boundary, which the book omits.

concepts.name: hypersurface element
concepts.definition: The covector-valued element dS_a = (1/3!) epsilon_{abcd} dtau^{bcd} on a three-dimensional hypersurface; with coordinates as parameters its components are the coordinate 3-volumes of the faces x^a = constant.
concepts.how_introduced: Introduced as the boundary measure in Gauss's theorem.
prerequisites: volume element of an m-dimensional subspace

concepts.name: Gauss's divergence theorem for vector densities
concepts.definition: For a weight +1 vector density on a four-dimensional region, the flux through the boundary hypersurface, integrated with dS_a, equals the volume integral of its ordinary divergence.
concepts.how_introduced: The m = 4 case of Stokes' theorem, drawn with Fig. 7.1.
prerequisites: divergence of a weight +1 vector density

concepts.name: covariant divergence theorem
concepts.definition: For any vector field T^a on a Lorentzian manifold, the integral of T^a sqrt(-g) dS_a over the boundary equals the integral of nabla_a T^a sqrt(-g) dOmega over the enclosed region.
concepts.how_introduced: Obtained by choosing the density sqrt(-g) T^a in Gauss's theorem and using (7.6) and (7.13) to replace the partial divergence by the covariant one.
prerequisites: Gauss's divergence theorem for vector densities
concepts.notes: Foundation for integral conservation laws (a covariantly divergence-free current gives a conserved charge) and for discarding boundary terms in Chapter 11.

concepts.name: functional
concepts.definition: A map that takes an entire function (drawn from some admissible class) as its input and returns a single real number; the action integral is the model case.
concepts.how_introduced: Opening definition of §7.5, used to frame the action.

concepts.name: action
concepts.definition: The functional I[y] = integral from x_1 to x_2 of L(y, y', x) dx whose stationary points are sought; for fields it is the integral of a Lagrangian density over a region of the manifold.
concepts.how_introduced: Posed as the basic problem of the calculus of variations: find the functions making I stationary (maxima, minima or saddle points). The unknown y(x) is called the dynamical variable (bold in the text), a name reused in Chapter 11 when g_ab becomes the dynamical variable.

concepts.name: Lagrangian
concepts.definition: The function L of the dependent variable, its first derivative and the independent variable whose integral forms the action.
concepts.how_introduced: Named alongside the action; the book calls L a functional of y, y' and x, although it is an ordinary function of those three arguments.

concepts.name: fundamental lemma of the calculus of variations
concepts.definition: If a continuous function phi(x) integrates to zero against every sufficiently smooth eta(x) that vanishes at both endpoints, then phi vanishes identically on the interval.
concepts.how_introduced: Set in a shaded box labelled Lemma and proved by contradiction: where phi has one sign, insert the polynomial bump eta = (x - xi_1)^4 (x - xi_2)^4 on that subinterval (zero elsewhere). The bump is only three times continuously differentiable, which is enough for the twice-differentiable test functions the lemma asks for.

concepts.name: variation of a function
concepts.definition: A small change delta y = y-bar - y = epsilon eta(x) of the dependent function with eta smooth and zero at the endpoints; the induced change in a functional to first order is delta I.
concepts.how_introduced: Defined in bold just before the first-order expansion of the action.

concepts.name: commutation of variation and differentiation
concepts.definition: The variation of the derivative equals the derivative of the variation, delta(y') = (delta y)', because both equal epsilon eta'.
concepts.how_introduced: Shown in one line by differentiating y-bar = y + epsilon eta; this is what allows integration by parts.

concepts.name: Euler-Lagrange equation
concepts.definition: The necessary condition dL/dy - d/dx(dL/dy') = 0 for a curve y(x) with fixed endpoints to make the action stationary; for several functions or fields there is one such equation per dependent variable.
concepts.how_introduced: Derived from first-order expansion, integration by parts, vanishing boundary term and the fundamental lemma.
prerequisites: fundamental lemma of the calculus of variations

concepts.name: functional derivative
concepts.definition: The Euler-Lagrange expression dL/dy - d/dx(dL/dy') regarded as a derivative of the action with respect to the function, so that delta I is its integral against delta y.
concepts.how_introduced: Introduced as shorthand that makes delta I = 0 and the Euler-Lagrange equation look like ordinary stationarity conditions.
formulas: \frac{\delta L}{\delta y} := \frac{\partial L}{\partial y} - \frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}x}\left(\frac{\partial L}{\partial y'}\right)
concepts.notes: Many texts attach the functional derivative to the action (delta I / delta y) rather than to L; the content is the same.

concepts.name: principle of stationary action
concepts.definition: Physical histories (or geometric curves such as geodesics) are those for which the first-order change of the action vanishes for all variations that are zero at the boundary.
concepts.how_introduced: Named in bold after the variational derivative is introduced; the section closes by claiming most physical theories can be specified by a Lagrangian whose Euler-Lagrange equations are the field equations.

concepts.name: Euler-Lagrange equations for several dependent variables
concepts.definition: When the action depends on n functions y_i(x) varied independently with fixed endpoints, stationarity requires a separate Euler-Lagrange equation for each y_i.
concepts.how_introduced: Stated as a straightforward generalization, repeating the one-variable structure with an index.

concepts.name: Lagrangian density
concepts.definition: A weight +1 scalar density built from fields y_A, their first partial derivatives and the coordinates, whose integral over a region of an n-dimensional manifold is the action of a field theory.
concepts.how_introduced: Given as the further generalization of the Euler-Lagrange framework to fields on a manifold.
concepts.notes: Weight +1 is required so that the integrand times dOmega is a scalar.

concepts.name: field equations from a variational principle
concepts.definition: For a Lagrangian density depending on fields and their first derivatives, the stationary-action conditions are dL/dy_A - (dL/dy_{A,b})_{,b} = 0 for each field; these are taken as the field equations of the theory.
concepts.how_introduced: Quoted without derivation at the end of §7.5, preparing for relativistic mechanics (Chapter 8) and the Einstein-Hilbert action (Chapter 11).
prerequisites: Euler-Lagrange equations for several dependent variables

concepts.name: metric geodesic as a curve of stationary interval
concepts.definition: The curve joining two points whose interval s (the integral of sqrt(g_ab xdot^a xdot^b) du) is unchanged to first order under all small variations fixed at the endpoints.
concepts.how_introduced: Named in bold ('metric geodesic') at the start of §7.6: the Euler-Lagrange machinery is applied with L = sqrt(g xdot xdot) so the action equals the interval, and the geodesic is the curve making it stationary with endpoints fixed.
prerequisites: Euler-Lagrange equations for several dependent variables
concepts.notes: Stationary, not necessarily minimal: timelike geodesics locally maximize proper time in Lorentzian signature, a fact not stated in this chapter.

concepts.name: geodesic equation with arbitrary parameter
concepts.definition: With a general parameter u, the stationary-interval condition gives xddot^a + Gamma^a_{bc} xdot^b xdot^c = (sddot/sdot) xdot^a, where s(u) is arc length; the right side only rescales the tangent and represents the parametrization, not a force.
concepts.how_introduced: Derived by multiplying the Euler-Lagrange equation by -2L, recasting in terms of L^2, and evaluating both sides.
prerequisites: metric geodesic as a curve of stationary interval

concepts.name: affine parameter
concepts.definition: A parameter along a geodesic for which the geodesic equation has no term proportional to the tangent; for non-null geodesics these are exactly the parameters s-bar = alpha s + beta with s the arc length, and for null geodesics any two affine parameters are likewise related linearly.
concepts.how_introduced: Revisited from Chapter 6: setting u = s removes the right-hand side of (7.42), and the null case is treated by analogy.

concepts.name: null geodesic
concepts.definition: A geodesic along which the interval between any two points is zero, so its tangent satisfies g_ab xdot^a xdot^b = 0; its general equation carries a lambda(u) xdot^a term that vanishes for affine parametrizations.
concepts.how_introduced: Raised as the case where L = 0 breaks the square-root derivation; the modified argument is explicitly omitted.

concepts.name: K-Lagrangian method for geodesics
concepts.definition: With an affine parameter, geodesics of any causal type are the solutions of the Euler-Lagrange equations for K = (1/2) g_ab xdot^a xdot^b; no square roots appear and the null case is included.
concepts.how_introduced: Summary recipe at the end of §7.6, after the square-root derivation has shown why the L^2 form and affine parameters are convenient; the justification is Exercise 7.7.
prerequisites: Euler-Lagrange equations for several dependent variables
metric geodesic as a curve of stationary interval
concepts.notes: Because K has no explicit u dependence, its Euler-Lagrange equations automatically conserve K along solutions (a first integral), which is why 2K can be fixed at 0 or plus/minus 1; the book asserts constancy without this explanation. Cyclic coordinates of K give further conserved momenta, as exploited in Chapter 16.

concepts.name: normalization of the geodesic tangent (2K = 0, +1, -1)
aliases: first integral of the geodesic equations
concepts.definition: Along an affinely parametrized geodesic 2K = g_ab xdot^a xdot^b is constant; it is chosen to be 0 for null geodesics, +1 for timelike geodesics parametrized by proper time s, and -1 for spacelike geodesics parametrized by proper distance sigma (in the book's +--- signature).
concepts.how_introduced: Stated with the K-Lagrangian recipe as the normalization to impose in practice.

concepts.name: reading off Christoffel symbols from geodesic equations
concepts.definition: Write the Euler-Lagrange equations of K for a given metric in the form xddot^a + (quadratic in xdot) = 0; the coefficient of xdot^b xdot^c is Gamma^a_{bc} when b = c and twice Gamma^a_{bc} when b differs from c, since the symmetric connection appears twice in the sum.
concepts.how_introduced: Mentioned in the last sentence of §7.6 as a very efficient alternative to the Christoffel formula; practised in Exercise 7.8 with the hint that Gamma is symmetric.
concepts.notes: The factor of 2 for mixed terms is the most common learner error and is only hinted at in the book.

concepts.name: Christoffel symbols of the first kind
concepts.definition: The combinations {bc,a} = (1/2)(d_c g_ba + d_b g_ca - d_a g_bc) of metric derivatives; raising the last index with g^{ad} gives the metric connection.
concepts.how_introduced: Recalled from Chapter 6 when evaluating the left side of the geodesic Euler-Lagrange equation.

concepts.name: discrete and continuous symmetries
concepts.definition: Symmetry transformations split into discrete ones such as reflections and continuous families such as translations and rotations; the continuous ones can be found systematically from Killing vectors.
concepts.how_introduced: Opening paragraph of §7.7 using Euclidean space as the familiar model.

concepts.name: diffeomorphism
concepts.definition: A smooth, invertible map of a manifold to itself whose inverse is also smooth.
concepts.how_introduced: Defined in bold as the kind of map used to move points and tensors in the discussion of symmetry.
concepts.notes: The text says smooth means infinitely differentiable; smoothness of the inverse is implicit.

concepts.name: active versus passive transformation
concepts.definition: A passive transformation relabels the same point with new coordinates; an active transformation moves the point (and tensors attached to it) to a different point while keeping one coordinate system. Formulas can look identical while meaning different things.
concepts.how_introduced: Emphasized immediately after the push-forward formula, contrasting it with the Chapter 5 coordinate-change law.

concepts.name: push-forward
concepts.definition: Using a diffeomorphism taking P to Q, the map that transports a covariant tensor T_ab at P to a tensor at Q by contracting with dx^c/dx-tilde^a factors, expressed in the one coordinate system x^a.
concepts.how_introduced: Defined by (7.49) with a warning that it resembles, but is not, a change of coordinates.
concepts.notes: For covariant tensors this uses the inverse map; modern texts usually describe covariant tensors as naturally pulled back.

concepts.name: pull-back
concepts.definition: The reverse transport of a covariant tensor from Q back to P using dx-tilde^c/dx^a factors.
concepts.how_introduced: Defined by (7.50) right after the push-forward and then used to state the symmetry condition.

concepts.name: symmetry of a tensor field
aliases: invariance of a tensor field under a map
concepts.definition: A diffeomorphism is a symmetry of a tensor field if pulling the field's value at the image point back to the original point reproduces the field's value there, for every point.
concepts.how_introduced: Built from the pull-back by evaluating the transported tensor on the field itself.

concepts.name: isometry
concepts.definition: A diffeomorphism that is a symmetry of the metric, so that all lengths, angles and intervals are preserved.
concepts.how_introduced: The metric case of the symmetry condition, singled out in bold; noted to be very complicated to solve directly.
concepts.notes: Chapter 15 adds that isometries form a group and uses it to define spherical symmetry.

concepts.name: infinitesimal transformation generated by a vector field
concepts.definition: The map x^a -> x^a + epsilon X^a(x) with small epsilon, which moves each point a short way along the vector field X; its Jacobian is delta^a_b + epsilon d_b X^a.
concepts.how_introduced: Introduced to linearize the isometry condition; called an infinitesimal coordinate transformation in the text although used actively.

concepts.name: Lie derivative of the metric
concepts.definition: L_X g_ab = X^e d_e g_ab + g_ad d_b X^d + g_bd d_a X^d, equivalently nabla_a X_b + nabla_b X_a for a metric connection; it measures how the metric changes when dragged along X.
concepts.how_introduced: Recognized as the order-epsilon bracket in the expanded isometry condition, referring back to the general Lie derivative formula (6.17).

concepts.name: Killing's equation
concepts.definition: The condition nabla_a X_b + nabla_b X_a = 0 (vanishing Lie derivative of the metric) on a vector field X; it is a tensor equation, so it holds in all coordinates if it holds in one.
concepts.how_introduced: Obtained by replacing partial with covariant derivatives in the Lie derivative of the metric and setting it to zero.

concepts.name: Killing vector field
concepts.definition: A vector field satisfying Killing's equation; moving points along its integral curves preserves the metric, so it encodes a continuous symmetry of the manifold.
concepts.how_introduced: Named in bold as any solution of Killing's equation and linked to Chapter 6's language of dragging: the metric is dragged into itself.
concepts.notes: In coordinates adapted so that X = d/dx^0, Killing's equation reduces to the metric components being independent of x^0 (used in Chapter 15).

concepts.name: theorem: Killing vectors generate infinitesimal isometries
concepts.definition: An infinitesimal isometry corresponds exactly to a vector field X^a with L_X g_ab = 0.
concepts.how_introduced: Boxed theorem summarizing §7.7.

concepts.name: generation of finite transformations from infinitesimal ones
concepts.definition: A continuous transformation connected to the identity can be assembled by integrating (composing infinitely many) infinitesimal transformations along a vector field, which is why it suffices to study Killing vectors.
concepts.how_introduced: Asserted without proof after the theorem to justify restricting attention to infinitesimal isometries.
prerequisites: infinitesimal transformation generated by a vector field
concepts.notes: Discrete isometries (reflections) and global issues such as incomplete flows are not captured by this statement.

concepts.name: Lie algebra of Killing vectors
aliases: closure of Killing vectors under brackets
concepts.definition: Constant-coefficient linear combinations of Killing vectors are Killing vectors, and the Lie bracket of two Killing vectors is again a Killing vector, so Killing vectors form a Lie algebra.
concepts.how_introduced: Left to Exercises 7.12 and 7.13, the latter via the operator identity L_X L_Y - L_Y L_X = L_[X,Y].

concepts.name: Killing vectors of Euclidean space
concepts.definition: Flat three-dimensional Euclidean space has six independent Killing vectors of the form X^a = omega^a_b x^b + t^a with omega antisymmetric: three translations and three rotations.
concepts.how_introduced: Exercise 7.11, with a hinted route through vanishing second derivatives; the Minkowski analogue follows in Exercise 8.5.

concepts.name: second-derivative identity for Killing vectors
concepts.definition: A Killing vector satisfies nabla_c nabla_b X_a = R_abcd X^d, so it is fixed everywhere (on a connected manifold) by its value and first derivative at one point; contracting gives g^{bc} nabla_b nabla_a X_c - R_ab X^b = 0 in the book's Exercise 7.14 form.
concepts.how_introduced: Exercises 7.14 and 7.15, using the commutator of covariant derivatives and the cyclic Riemann identity.
concepts.notes: The consequence that an n-dimensional space has at most n(n+1)/2 independent Killing vectors is not drawn in this chapter.

key_equations.name: Transformation law of a tensor density
key_equations.latex: \mathfrak{T}'^{a\cdots}_{b\cdots} = J^{W}\frac{\partial x'^a}{\partial x^c}\cdots\frac{\partial x^d}{\partial x'^b}\cdots\mathfrak{T}^{c\cdots}_{d\cdots},\qquad J = \left|\frac{\partial x^a}{\partial x'^b}\right|
key_equations.meaning: A density of weight W transforms as a tensor times the W-th power of the Jacobian of old with respect to new coordinates.
key_equations.symbols: W weight; J Jacobian determinant; primes mark new coordinates and components

key_equations.name: Covariant derivative of a tensor density
key_equations.meaning: Book's convention: tensor-like connection terms plus a correction proportional to the weight and the contracted connection.

key_equations.name: Covariant derivative of a vector density
key_equations.meaning: Explicit instance of (7.2) for one contravariant index.

key_equations.name: Divergence of a weight +1 vector density
key_equations.meaning: For W = +1 the connection terms cancel on contraction, so the covariant divergence needs only partial derivatives.

key_equations.name: Sample alternating-symbol values
key_equations.meaning: Illustrates the parity rule: even permutations +1, odd -1, repeated index 0.

key_equations.name: Determinant from alternating symbols
key_equations.meaning: Writes the determinant as a fully contracted product, showing it is a weight +2 scalar density.

key_equations.name: Determinant transformation
key_equations.latex: T'_{ab}(x') = \frac{\partial x^c}{\partial x'^a}\frac{\partial x^d}{\partial x'^b}T_{cd}(x)\;\Longrightarrow\;\det T' = J^2\det T
key_equations.meaning: Consistency check of the weight +2 claim directly from the transformation law.

key_equations.name: Determinant of a contravariant tensor
key_equations.meaning: Lower-index symbols (weight -1) give a weight -2 scalar density. The reading copy garbles T^{ab} as T^{ub}; the print is correct.

key_equations.name: Generalized Kronecker delta (two pairs)
key_equations.latex: \delta^{ab}_{cd} = \begin{vmatrix}\delta^a_c & \delta^b_c\\ \delta^a_d & \delta^b_d\end{vmatrix} = \begin{cases}+1 & a\neq b,\ a=c,\ b=d\\ -1 & a\neq b,\ a=d,\ b=c\\ 0 & \text{otherwise}\end{cases}
key_equations.meaning: Antisymmetrized identity map on pairs of indices.

key_equations.name: Generalized Kronecker delta (three pairs)
key_equations.meaning: Determinant form; lower indices label rows. The reading copy misprints the middle row with subscript c; the rendered page shows e.

key_equations.name: Epsilon-epsilon contractions in four dimensions
key_equations.meaning: Each extra contracted pair multiplies by the number of ways to permute the contracted indices.

key_equations.name: Metric transformation law
key_equations.meaning: Starting point for the density character of g.

key_equations.name: Weight of the metric determinant
key_equations.meaning: g is a weight +2 scalar density, negative for Lorentzian metrics.

key_equations.name: Weight of sqrt(-g)
key_equations.meaning: sqrt(-g) is a weight +1 scalar density, the factor that turns tensors into integrable densities.

key_equations.name: Divergence of sqrt(-g) times a vector
key_equations.meaning: Special case of (7.3) for the weight +1 density sqrt(-g) T^a.

key_equations.name: Inverse matrix via cofactors
key_equations.meaning: Standard linear-algebra formula used in the determinant-derivative digression.
key_equations.symbols: a = det A; A^{ij} cofactor of a_ij; b^{ij} inverse

key_equations.name: Row expansion of a determinant
key_equations.meaning: Cofactors of row i contain no entries of row i, enabling (7.8).

key_equations.name: Derivative of a determinant with respect to an entry
key_equations.meaning: The sensitivity of a determinant to one entry is that entry's cofactor.

key_equations.name: Chain rule for a coordinate-dependent determinant
key_equations.latex: \frac{\partial a}{\partial x^k} = \frac{\partial a}{\partial a_{ij}}\frac{\partial a_{ij}}{\partial x^k} = A^{ij}\frac{\partial a_{ij}}{\partial x^k} = a\,b^{ji}\frac{\partial a_{ij}}{\partial x^k}
key_equations.meaning: Jacobi's formula in component form.

key_equations.name: Derivative of the metric determinant
key_equations.meaning: Jacobi's formula specialized to the symmetric metric.

key_equations.name: Contracted connection and the metric determinant
key_equations.meaning: Links the trace of the metric connection to the logarithmic derivative of g: Gamma^a_{ac} = d_c ln sqrt(-g).

key_equations.name: Covariant derivative of g from (7.2)
key_equations.meaning: Weight +2 scalar-density case of the density derivative.

key_equations.name: Covariant constancy of g
key_equations.meaning: Follows from (7.10); tied to the chosen density convention.

key_equations.name: Partial derivative of sqrt(-g)
key_equations.meaning: Square-root version of (7.10).

key_equations.name: Covariant constancy of sqrt(-g)
key_equations.meaning: sqrt(-g) behaves like a constant under covariant differentiation.

key_equations.name: Pulling sqrt(-g) through nabla
key_equations.meaning: Factors of sqrt(-g) (and g) commute with covariant derivatives, like metric factors.

key_equations.name: Sum of scalar values is invariant
key_equations.meaning: Motivates integration: scalars at different points can be added invariantly.

key_equations.name: Integral of a weight +1 scalar density
key_equations.meaning: Invariant because Phi dOmega has total weight zero.
key_equations.symbols: Phi weight +1 scalar density; dOmega weight -1 volume element

key_equations.name: Volume element of an m-dimensional subspace

key_equations.meaning: Antisymmetrized oriented m-volume spanned by coordinate tangent vectors; a contravariant tensor that is parameter-invariant.
key_equations.symbols: u^i parameters on the subspace x^a(u^i)

key_equations.name: Integral over a subspace
key_equations.meaning: Contracting a covariant rank-m tensor with the element gives an integrable scalar.

key_equations.name: Stokes' theorem
key_equations.meaning: Boundary integral equals the region integral of the derivative; orientation conventions are left implicit.

key_equations.name: Gauss's theorem for a weight +1 vector density
key_equations.meaning: Four-dimensional divergence theorem with ordinary divergence of a density.

key_equations.name: Hypersurface element
key_equations.meaning: Dualizes the 3-volume element into a covector on the boundary.

key_equations.name: Four-volume element
key_equations.meaning: Scalar 4-volume element of weight -1 built from the parametrized element.

key_equations.name: Coordinate volume element
key_equations.meaning: dOmega when the coordinates themselves are the parameters; a weight -1 scalar density.

key_equations.name: Coordinate hypersurface elements
key_equations.meaning: Component a is the coordinate 3-volume of a face x^a = constant; alternating signs from epsilon are absorbed into orientation.

key_equations.name: Density divergence becomes covariant divergence
key_equations.meaning: Chain combining (7.6) and (7.13).

key_equations.name: Covariant divergence theorem
key_equations.meaning: Flux of a vector field through a closed hypersurface equals the invariant integral of its covariant divergence.

key_equations.name: Action functional
key_equations.meaning: The quantity whose stationary values are sought.

key_equations.name: Bump function in the lemma
key_equations.meaning: Smooth enough (continuous second derivatives), positive inside, zero outside: isolates a region where phi has one sign.

key_equations.name: Varied path
key_equations.meaning: One-parameter family of comparison paths.
key_equations.symbols: epsilon small; eta zero at endpoints

key_equations.name: Variation
key_equations.meaning: Definition of the variation symbol.

key_equations.name: Variation commutes with differentiation
key_equations.meaning: delta and d/dx commute on y.

key_equations.name: First-order change of the action
key_equations.meaning: Taylor expansion to first order in epsilon.

key_equations.meaning: Change in the action is the Euler-Lagrange expression integrated against the variation.

key_equations.name: Euler-Lagrange equation
key_equations.meaning: Condition for a stationary curve.

key_equations.name: Variational derivative

key_equations.meaning: Square-root-free Lagrangian for geodesics.

figures.label: Fig. 7.1
figures.caption_paraphrase: A four-dimensional region Omega together with the closed hypersurface that bounds it.
figures.visual_description: A single closed, smooth, irregular outline (roughly potato-shaped, with a gentle dent on the upper left) drawn in a thick black line on white. The label Omega sits inside near the centre. A short horizontal leader line runs from the right-hand edge of the outline to the label for the boundary, written as partial Omega. There is no shading, no normal vectors, no arrows showing orientation, and no indication of time or light cones.
