concepts: Gauss's divergence theorem for vector densities

redesign.idea: Flux ledger in curved coordinates: a 2D plane carrying a selectable metric (flat Cartesian, flat polar chart, or a curved surface chart such as the sphere) where the learner sketches or drags a closed region and picks a vector field. Outward normal arrows along the boundary are coloured by local flux; the interior is shaded by the covariant divergence. Two running totals, the boundary flux with the sqrt(g) measure and the interior integral of nabla_a T^a sqrt(g) d^2x, update live and agree. A toggle drops the sqrt(g) factors (or uses the partial divergence of T^a instead of the density), and the totals visibly disagree. A 3D companion mode stacks the region into a spacetime slab (two spacelike slices plus a timelike wall) to show a conserved charge as flux balance.
redesign.interaction: Drag boundary control points; choose metric chart and vector field from presets or enter components; toggle sqrt(g) on/off; in 3D mode slide the upper time slice and watch charge in the slab change only by wall flux.

worked_examples.label: Inline check: divergence of a weight +1 vector density (§7.1)
worked_examples.problem: Show that for a vector density of weight +1 the covariant divergence reduces to the partial divergence.
worked_examples.method: Write the vector-density covariant derivative from (7.2), set W = +1, contract c with a, and relabel dummy indices in the connection terms.
worked_examples.key_insight: The +Gamma^a_{ba} T^b term and the -Gamma^b_{ba} T^a term are the same after renaming, provided the connection is symmetric, so they cancel.
concepts: covariant derivative of a tensor density
divergence of a weight +1 vector density

worked_examples.label: Inline derivation: weight of a determinant (§7.2)
worked_examples.problem: Determine the transformation character of det(T_ab) for a covariant rank-2 tensor.
worked_examples.method: Express the determinant with two upper-index alternating symbols (7.4) and add weights; cross-check by taking determinants of the tensor transformation law.
worked_examples.key_insight: Two weight +1 symbols contracted with tensors give weight +2, matching det T' = J^2 det T.
worked_examples.result: det(T_ab) is a scalar density of weight +2; det(T^ab) has weight -2.
concepts: determinant of a rank-2 tensor via alternating symbols

worked_examples.label: Inline derivation: derivative of a determinant and of g (§7.3)
worked_examples.problem: Find the partial derivative of the determinant of a coordinate-dependent matrix, and specialize to the metric.
worked_examples.method: Expand the determinant along a fixed row; since that row's cofactors do not contain its entries, differentiate to get the cofactor; apply the chain rule and the inverse-matrix formula (7.7); use symmetry of g_ab.
worked_examples.key_insight: Cofactor expansion makes the dependence on each entry linear, so the derivative with respect to an entry is read off immediately.
worked_examples.result: d_c g = g g^{ab} d_c g_ab (7.9).

worked_examples.label: Inline derivation: covariant constancy of g and sqrt(-g) (§7.3)
worked_examples.problem: Show that g and sqrt(-g) have vanishing covariant derivatives.
worked_examples.method: Substitute the metric-connection expression (6.77) for d_c g_ab into (7.9), contract with g^{ab} to get 2 g Gamma^a_{ac}; then apply (7.2) with W = 2 for g and W = 1 for sqrt(-g).
worked_examples.key_insight: The trace of the metric connection is exactly the logarithmic derivative of sqrt(-g), which is what the density correction term subtracts.
worked_examples.result: nabla_c g = 0 (7.11), nabla_c sqrt(-g) = 0 (7.12), and sqrt(-g) commutes with nabla (7.13).
concepts: covariant constancy of g and sqrt(-g)

worked_examples.label: Inline derivation: covariant divergence theorem (§7.4)
worked_examples.problem: Turn Gauss's theorem for densities into a statement about an ordinary vector field.
worked_examples.method: Choose the weight +1 density sqrt(-g) T^a in (7.19); rewrite its partial divergence as a covariant divergence using (7.6), then pull sqrt(-g) out with (7.13).
worked_examples.key_insight: Weight +1 densities are exactly the objects whose partial and covariant divergences coincide, and sqrt(-g) is the canonical converter from tensors to such densities.
worked_examples.result: Integral over the boundary of T^a sqrt(-g) dS_a equals integral over Omega of nabla_a T^a sqrt(-g) dOmega (7.24).

worked_examples.label: Inline proof: fundamental lemma of the calculus of variations (§7.5)
worked_examples.problem: Prove that a continuous phi orthogonal to every admissible eta must vanish.
worked_examples.method: Assume phi(xi) > 0; continuity gives an interval around xi where phi > 0; choose eta equal to (x - xi_1)^4 (x - xi_2)^4 inside and zero outside; the integral is then strictly positive, a contradiction. Repeat for phi(xi) < 0.
worked_examples.key_insight: Admissible test functions can be localized to any small interval, so a function that integrates to zero against all of them has nowhere to hide a nonzero value.
concepts: fundamental lemma of the calculus of variations

worked_examples.label: Inline derivation: Euler-Lagrange equation (§7.5)
worked_examples.problem: Find the condition for y(x) with fixed endpoints to make the action (7.25) stationary.
worked_examples.method: Vary y by epsilon eta, show delta commutes with d/dx, expand L to first order, integrate the eta' term by parts, drop the boundary term, and apply the lemma.
worked_examples.key_insight: Integration by parts moves all dependence onto eta itself, so stationarity for arbitrary eta forces the coefficient of eta to vanish pointwise.

worked_examples.label: Inline derivation: geodesic equation from stationary interval (§7.6)
worked_examples.problem: Derive the geodesic equation from the Lagrangian L = sqrt(g_ab xdot^a xdot^b) with an arbitrary parameter u.
worked_examples.method: Multiply the Euler-Lagrange equations by -2L and rewrite in terms of L^2 with a residual term 2 (dL/dxdot)(dL/du); evaluate the L^2 side to get 2 g_ab xddot^b + 2 {bc,a} xdot^b xdot^c; evaluate the residual using L = ds/du; equate, halve, raise with g^{ad}.
worked_examples.key_insight: The square-root Lagrangian is reparametrization invariant, so its Euler-Lagrange equations cannot fix the parameter; that freedom shows up as a term along the tangent which disappears exactly when u is an affine function of s.
worked_examples.result: xddot^a + Gamma^a_{bc} xdot^b xdot^c = (sddot/sdot) xdot^a (7.42); with u = s, (7.43).
concepts: metric geodesic as a curve of stationary interval

worked_examples.label: Inline derivation: Killing's equation (§7.7)
worked_examples.problem: Simplify the finite isometry condition (7.52) for a transformation close to the identity.
worked_examples.method: Insert x-tilde = x + epsilon X(x) and its Jacobian, Taylor expand g_cd at the displaced point, multiply out and keep terms of order epsilon; recognize the bracket as the Lie derivative (7.54) and convert to covariant derivatives with (6.74) and (6.58).
worked_examples.key_insight: Linearizing turns an intractable functional equation for a finite map into a linear first-order PDE for a vector field.
worked_examples.result: nabla_b X_a + nabla_a X_b = 0 (7.55); infinitesimal isometries are generated by Killing vectors.
concepts: infinitesimal transformation generated by a vector field

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: Adding up scalar readings taken at different places
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Because each observer agrees on a scalar's value at their own point, a sum of such values is observer-independent, which suggests integration should work provided the integrand times the volume element is a genuine scalar.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: Explains why scalars are candidates but not why the volume element spoils invariance; the weight bookkeeping is still needed.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Scatter sample points in a region under two coordinate grids; show the Riemann sum of phi times coordinate cell volume changing between grids until each cell volume is multiplied by sqrt(g).

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: The alternating symbol as a many-index cousin of the Kronecker delta
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Frames epsilon as a familiar constant array of 0 and plus/minus 1 whose entries are the same in every chart, then reveals that unlike delta it is not a tensor but a density.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: Delta is a genuine tensor; the parallel can mislead learners into treating epsilon as one, especially when raising and lowering indices.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: A functional is a function whose input is a whole function
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Reduces the calculus of variations to ordinary stationarity: vary the input curve slightly and demand no first-order change in the output number.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: Hides the infinite-dimensional subtleties (admissible function classes, existence of extremals, sufficient conditions).
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Draggable curve between fixed pins with a live bar showing I[y]; a slider for epsilon along a chosen bump eta plots I(epsilon), which has zero slope at epsilon = 0 only for the Euler-Lagrange solution.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: Translations, rotations and reflections of ordinary Euclidean space
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Grounds abstract metric symmetries in the familiar rigid motions and uses them to separate discrete from continuous symmetries.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: Euclidean space is maximally symmetric; generic spacetimes have few or no Killing vectors, and in Lorentzian signature boosts join the list.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Toggle between the plane, the sphere, and a lumpy surface; show which rigid slides keep a painted grid of small circles undistorted.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: The metric is dragged into itself
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Reuses the Chapter 6 picture of Lie dragging: flowing along a Killing field carries the metric onto an identical copy of itself.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: Requires the learner already to have a working image of Lie dragging; the book gives no new picture here.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Draw unit-circle indicatrices of the metric on a grid, then flow them along a chosen vector field; for a Killing field they arrive matching the indicatrices already painted at the destination, for other fields they arrive squashed.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: sqrt(-g) behaves like a metric factor under covariant differentiation
analogies_and_intuitions.target_concept: covariant constancy of g and sqrt(-g)
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Tells the reader that the same freedom to move g_ab through nabla extends to g and sqrt(-g), which is what simplifies the divergence theorem and later action calculations.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: Holds only with the book's density derivative convention and a metric connection.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: The coordinate volume element d^4x is an invariant, so the integral of a scalar field over d^4x is coordinate independent.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: d^4x is a scalar density of weight -1; one needs a weight +1 factor such as sqrt(-g) to make the integrand a scalar.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: In Cartesian coordinates on flat space the Jacobian correction is invisible, and physics courses often write d^3x without comment.
concepts: volume element as a scalar density of weight -1

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: The divergence of any vector field can be computed as the plain sum of partial derivatives d_a T^a.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Only a weight +1 vector density has connection-free divergence; for a vector field use (1/sqrt(-g)) d_a(sqrt(-g) T^a).
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: (7.3) looks like a general statement and Cartesian intuition suggests divergence is just partial derivatives.
concepts: divergence of a weight +1 vector density

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: The lower-index alternating symbol is obtained from the upper one by lowering indices with the metric.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Both are defined with the same numerical values in every chart and have weights +1 and -1; lowering with g_ab would instead give g times epsilon_{abcd}, which is negative in Lorentzian signature.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: For genuine tensors raising and lowering with the metric is automatic, and index notation makes it look allowed.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: The push-forward formula (7.49) is just a coordinate transformation.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: It moves a tensor from one point to another while keeping a single coordinate system; it is active, whereas the Chapter 5 formula relabels the same point.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: The two formulas contain identical Jacobian factors.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: The square-root variational derivation of geodesics covers light rays too.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: For null curves L = 0 and the division by L fails; the null equation must be obtained by a modified argument, conveniently via the K-Lagrangian.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: The final geodesic equation looks the same for all causal types.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Stationary action means minimum action, so geodesics are always shortest paths.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: The book explicitly lists maxima, minima and saddle points as stationary values. (Tutor addition, not in this chapter: timelike geodesics in spacetime locally maximize proper time rather than minimizing it.)
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: The name 'least action' and Euclidean experience with straight lines as shortest paths.
concepts: metric geodesic as a curve of stationary interval

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: The K-Lagrangian gives geodesics with any choice of parameter.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Its Euler-Lagrange equations produce affinely parametrized geodesics; with a non-affine parameter the extra tangent term of (7.42) is missing.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: The square-root Lagrangian is parameter-independent, and the switch to K is presented as a mere convenience.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: A Killing vector exists only when the metric components visibly do not depend on some coordinate.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Killing's equation is a tensor equation; independence of a coordinate is what it looks like in adapted coordinates, but symmetries such as rotations in Cartesian coordinates show no such independence.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Standard metrics are written in adapted coordinates (t, phi) where the symmetry is a missing variable.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Every isometry is generated by a Killing vector.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Killing vectors generate continuous families connected to the identity; discrete isometries such as reflections are not obtained this way.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: The chapter's theorem and the remark about building finite transformations are easy to over-read.
concepts: generation of finite transformations from infinitesimal ones

thought_experiments.name: Wiggling a path with its ends pinned
thought_experiments.setup: Take a candidate curve y(x) between two fixed points and add a small bump epsilon eta(x) that vanishes at the ends; ask how the action changes as epsilon is dialled through zero.
thought_experiments.lesson: A stationary curve is one where the first-order change vanishes for every such bump, which forces the Euler-Lagrange expression to vanish pointwise.
concepts: fundamental lemma of the calculus of variations
thought_experiments.app_idea: Learner drags a localized bump along a trial path and sees the local sign of the Euler-Lagrange residual as a colour; the action decreases when the bump is pushed in the direction the colour indicates.

thought_experiments.name: Sliding every point along a vector field and comparing metrics
thought_experiments.setup: Move each point P a short distance along X to Q, bring the metric at Q back to P by pull-back, and compare with the metric originally at P.
thought_experiments.lesson: If the two agree to first order for every point, the flow is an isometry and X satisfies Killing's equation.
thought_experiments.app_idea: On a sphere, choose a vector field (rotation about the axis, or a poleward flow); ghost copies of small circles are pulled back and overlaid on originals, with a mismatch meter.

applications_and_observations.topic: Orbits and light paths around a spherical mass via the K-Lagrangian (forward use)
applications_and_observations.details: The K-Lagrangian recipe of §7.6 is the method the book later uses for Schwarzschild geodesics, where cyclic coordinates t and phi give conserved energy and angular momentum; this underpins the perihelion advance of Mercury and light-bending calculations in Chapter 16.

applications_and_observations.topic: Symmetries of flat space and of symmetric spacetimes (forward use)
applications_and_observations.details: Killing vectors from §7.7 define stationary spacetimes (a timelike Killing vector) and spherically symmetric ones (three rotational Killing vectors with 2-sphere orbits) in Chapter 15, the setting for stars and non-rotating black holes; flat Euclidean 3-space has six Killing vectors (Exercise 7.11) and Minkowski space ten (Exercise 8.5).
applications_and_observations.key_numbers: Euclidean 3-space: 6 Killing vectors (3 translations, 3 rotations); Minkowski spacetime: 10 (Poincare group).

notation_and_conventions.convention: Tensor densities are written in gothic (fraktur) type, e.g. a gothic T^a.
notation_and_conventions.notes: Chapter 11 extends this: a gothic version of a tensor means the tensor multiplied by sqrt(-g).

notation_and_conventions.convention: J = |dx^a/dx'^b| (old with respect to new), so a weight-W density picks up J^W; hence g has weight +2, sqrt(-g) weight +1, epsilon^{abcd} weight +1, epsilon_{abcd} and d^4x weight -1.
notation_and_conventions.notes: Some texts define weight with the inverse Jacobian, reversing every sign; check before combining sources.

notation_and_conventions.convention: Correction term is -W Gamma^d_{dc} times the density.
notation_and_conventions.notes: Chosen so that epsilon, g and sqrt(-g) are covariantly constant.

notation_and_conventions.convention: Coordinate indices now run 0, 1, 2, 3 with x^0 the time-like coordinate.
epsilon^{0123} = +1 and epsilon_{0123} = +1, the same numerical values in every coordinate system; they are not related by index lowering.
Written as determinants of ordinary deltas with the upper index fixed by column and the lower index by row.
Metrics of 'negative signature' (+,-,-,-, signature -2) are used later, so g < 0 and sqrt(-g) is used rather than sqrt(g).
notation_and_conventions.notes: Timelike tangent vectors have positive squared length in this convention.

notation_and_conventions.convention: := marks a definition (e.g. delta y := y-bar - y, d^4x := dx^0 dx^1 dx^2 dx^3).
A comma in a subscript denotes a partial derivative: y_{A,b} = d_b y_A, T^a_{,a} = d_a T^a.
Prime means d/dx in the calculus-of-variations sections; a dot means d/du along a curve in §7.6.
delta y is the variation of a function, delta I the first-order change in the action, and delta L / delta y the variational (Euler-Lagrange) derivative of the Lagrangian.
s denotes proper time (arc length) along timelike curves with 2K = +1; sigma denotes proper distance along spacelike curves with 2K = -1.

notation_and_conventions.item: Christoffel symbols of the first kind
notation_and_conventions.convention: {bc,a} as in (6.63); Gamma^a_{bc} obtained by raising with g^{ad}.
Upright L with subscript vector, L_X.
A tilde marks the coordinates of the image point and quantities transported to it: x-tilde^a, T-tilde_ab.
In Exercise 7.11 distinct Killing vectors are labelled by a numeral set above the symbol, X with overset i.
Used loosely for any manifold carrying a metric, including the indefinite (Lorentzian) case; §7.3 speaks of a Riemannian manifold and in the next breath of negative-signature metrics.
notation_and_conventions.notes: Modern usage reserves 'Riemannian' for positive-definite metrics and says pseudo- or semi-Riemannian otherwise; warn learners reading other sources.

notation_and_conventions.convention: The function(s) y(x), y_i(x) or fields y_A(x) being varied in an action are called dynamical variables (bold in §7.5).
notation_and_conventions.notes: Chapter 11 treats g_ab as the dynamical variable of the Einstein Lagrangian.
A quick guide to what the authors consider must-remember.

margin_notes.summary: Admits that the covariant derivative of a density can be defined in more than one way before fixing the -W Gamma convention.
The vanishing covariant derivatives of both alternating symbols are offered as one motivation for the density derivative convention (proof left as Exercise 7.2).
Forward pointer: negative-signature metrics will be used in later chapters, which is why -g rather than g appears under the square root.
Remarks that nabla g = 0 is again closely tied to the chosen density derivative definition.
Stokes' theorem is identified with the ordinary Stokes theorem for a region of R^n once written in terms of the parameters.
§7.5 is flagged as a digression included for completeness, with a forward pointer to its use for geodesics in §7.6 and its wider importance later in the book.
Closes §7.5 with the programmatic claim that essentially every physical theory can be packaged as a choice of Lagrangian, its Euler-Lagrange equations then serving as the field equations.
The modified variational argument for null geodesics is explicitly omitted and only the resulting equation is quoted.
The K-Lagrangian approach is announced as the method used for geodesics throughout the rest of the book.
Justifies studying only infinitesimal isometries by asserting, without proof, that continuous finite transformations can be built by integrating infinitesimal ones.
Further reading refers back to the Chapter 5 list and names ten works ranging from Synge and Schild to Penrose and Rindler.

notable.summary: Apply the density covariant derivative (7.2) to both alternating symbols and show the results vanish identically.
notable.why_notable: The four connection terms acting on epsilon^{abcd} sum to Gamma^f_{fe} epsilon^{abcd}, which the -W Gamma term cancels for any connection; this is the cleanest justification of the book's convention.

notable.summary: Adapt the determinant-derivative argument to the Jacobian matrix, then use it to prove from first principles that the ordinary divergence of a weight +1 vector density transforms as a weight +1 scalar density.
notable.why_notable: Supplies the proof the text defers in §7.1 and shows why second derivatives of the coordinate change cancel exactly for weight +1.

notable.summary: Write the Euler-Lagrange equations for a simple quadratic Lagrangian in one variable and for a coupled two-variable Lagrangian with explicit x dependence.
notable.why_notable: The only drill on the raw Euler-Lagrange machinery before it is used for geodesics; part (i) gives y'' = y.

notable.summary: Repeat the geodesic variational argument for spacelike curves and show that, with an affine parameter, (7.41) collapses to the K-Lagrangian equations.
notable.why_notable: Justifies the recipe the book uses for every later geodesic calculation; the hint that dL/du = 0 for affine u is the key.

notable.summary: Use the K-Lagrangian to get geodesic equations for the general time-dependent spherically symmetric metric of Exercise 6.32 and read off its Christoffel symbols, checking against the direct computation.
notable.why_notable: Demonstrates the efficiency claim on the metric that later becomes Schwarzschild; the factor of two for mixed index pairs is the trap. Keyed to §7.7 in print though it uses §7.6.

notable.summary: Find every Killing vector of a two-dimensional diagonal metric whose components depend on one coordinate only.
notable.why_notable: Shows that an obvious translation symmetry may be the only one: the metric's Gaussian curvature is non-constant, so only multiples of the y-translation survive (tutor's own check).

notable.summary: Solve Killing's equation for flat Euclidean 3-space by showing all second derivatives of X vanish, obtain six independent fields, compute their mutual brackets, and interpret them as translations and rotations.
notable.why_notable: Builds the Euclidean group's Lie algebra from scratch; the Minkowski version (Exercise 8.5) gives the Poincare group.

notable.summary: Verify the commutator identity for Lie derivatives on scalars, vectors and covectors, use it to prove the bracket of Killing vectors is Killing, and generate a third planar Killing field from two given ones.
notable.why_notable: Establishes that symmetries form a Lie algebra; the final part yields the y-translation as the bracket of the x-translation and the rotation.

notable.summary: Write the commutator of two covariant derivatives on a covector in terms of curvature and use Killing's equation to derive a contracted wave-type identity involving the Ricci tensor.
notable.why_notable: First link between symmetry and curvature; its hint is reused for the Minkowski Killing vectors in Exercise 8.5.

notable.summary: Use the cyclic identity of the Riemann tensor to show that second covariant derivatives of a Killing vector are fixed by curvature acting on the vector.
notable.why_notable: Key to proving a Killing field is determined by its value and derivative at one point, and reused in Chapter 10 (Killing vectors and geodesic deviation).

difficulty.notes: Three unrelated toolkits are packed into eighteen pages with almost no pictures and no worked numerical examples. The density and determinant material is mechanically heavy but conceptually modest; the calculus of variations is gentle and fully proved; the geodesic derivation is the longest index calculation; §7.7 is short but conceptually slippery because active and passive language are mixed. Stokes' theorem and the null-geodesic case are quoted rather than explained, and orientation is never discussed.

teaching_gems.gem: Weight bookkeeping: tag every object with its Jacobian power, then read off invariance of sqrt(-g) d^4x, Phi dOmega or det T by adding weights to zero.
teaching_gems.why_effective: Replaces a page of transformation-law algebra with integer arithmetic and explains in one stroke why the invariant volume needs sqrt(-g).
teaching_gems.app_idea: Coordinate-warp playground in 2D: deform a grid (polar, stretched, sheared) and display for one cell the coordinate area (weight -1), sqrt(g) (weight +1) and their product; a weight counter badge shows the sum and only the zero-weight product stays constant as the warp slider moves.

teaching_gems.gem: Differentiate a determinant by expanding along a row: the derivative with respect to an entry is its cofactor, giving d_c g = g g^{ab} d_c g_ab and hence Gamma^a_{ac} = d_c ln sqrt(-g).
teaching_gems.why_effective: A two-line linear-algebra fact unlocks the connection trace, the divergence formula and later the variation of sqrt(-g) in the action.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Matrix sensitivity widget: a 3x3 matrix with draggable entries; nudging one entry shows the change in the determinant next to the cofactor predicted value, then the same demo on a polar-coordinate metric computes Gamma^a_{ar} and ln sqrt(g) side by side.

teaching_gems.gem: Prove the fundamental lemma with an explicit localized bump (x - xi_1)^4 (x - xi_2)^4.
teaching_gems.why_effective: Makes the key step of the calculus of variations concrete and visual instead of an appeal to arbitrariness.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Plot a draggable phi(x); the learner positions and resizes a bump eta, watching the integral of phi eta; any nonzero spot of phi can be trapped to give a nonzero integral.

teaching_gems.gem: Derive geodesics from the square-root Lagrangian first, exposing the (sddot/sdot) xdot^a reparametrization term, then switch to K = (1/2) g xdot xdot.
teaching_gems.why_effective: Learners see why the K method is legitimate (affine parameter), what it silently fixes, and why it also handles null curves.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Geodesic on a sphere or in a Schwarzschild equatorial plane drawn with beads at equal parameter steps; switching between an affine and a distorted parameter redistributes the beads and turns on a tangent-direction 'fake force' arrow equal to (sddot/sdot) xdot, while the path itself is unchanged.

teaching_gems.gem: Read off Christoffel symbols from the Euler-Lagrange equations of K instead of evaluating the Christoffel formula term by term.
teaching_gems.why_effective: Turns the most tedious calculation in early GR into a short, checkable procedure and prepares for Schwarzschild orbits.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Christoffel reader: learner types a diagonal metric (2-sphere, polar plane, Schwarzschild); the app shows K, each Euler-Lagrange equation, highlights each xdot^b xdot^c coefficient and asks the learner to enter Gamma, flagging the factor of 2 on mixed terms.

teaching_gems.gem: Obtain Killing's equation by expanding the finite isometry condition to first order and recognizing the Lie derivative of the metric.
teaching_gems.why_effective: Connects symmetry to a linear PDE through a routine Taylor expansion and reuses the Chapter 6 Lie derivative, so nothing new has to be memorized.
teaching_gems.app_idea: On a chosen surface, the learner sketches a vector field; small metric circles are flowed along it for a short time and compared with the circles at the destination; a heat map of |L_X g| shows where the field fails to be Killing, and presets include rotation of a sphere and translations of the plane.

teaching_gems.gem: Active versus passive: identical Jacobian formulas can mean relabelling a point or moving a tensor to another point.
teaching_gems.why_effective: Pre-empts the pervasive confusion between coordinate freedom (diffeomorphism invariance) and genuine symmetry.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Split-screen: left pane redraws the grid under a map with points fixed (passive), right pane moves a painted arrow across a fixed grid (active); the component readouts are identical in both panes.

teaching_gems.gem: Covariant divergence theorem as the reward of densities: flux of T^a sqrt(-g) through a boundary equals the invariant integral of nabla_a T^a.
teaching_gems.why_effective: Gives the abstract density machinery an immediate physical use (conservation laws) and a picture.
teaching_gems.app_idea: See the Fig. 7.1 redesign: flux ledger in curvilinear coordinates with a sqrt(g) toggle.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: The sign of density weights is a convention: this book uses the Jacobian of old with respect to new coordinates, so sqrt(-g) has weight +1; other texts reverse it.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Learners mixing sources get contradictory weights and doubt their understanding.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: State the convention up front and anchor it with the single fact that sqrt(-g) d^4x must be invariant.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: The two alternating symbols are defined numerically and are not related by the metric; this is never said.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Raising or lowering epsilon with g_ab in Lorentzian signature introduces a silent minus sign (and a factor of g).
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Contrast the symbol with the Levi-Civita tensor sqrt(-g) epsilon_{abcd} and show the sign flip explicitly.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Stokes' theorem (7.18) is quoted without proof or orientation conventions, under a 'simply connected' hypothesis; with the given index placement the two-dimensional case yields Green's theorem only if the boundary is traversed in the sense opposite to the usual counter-clockwise one (tutor's own check).
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Sign errors in flux calculations and confusion about which hypotheses really matter (orientability and compactness rather than simple connectivity).
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Work the m = 2 case explicitly in the plane and state the orientation rule; mention the differential-forms version as the clean statement.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: (7.23) lists coordinate hypersurface elements with all plus signs, suppressing the alternating signs that epsilon_{abcd} produces.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Learners who compute dS_a from (7.20) find sign discrepancies and cannot reconcile them.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Explain that the components represent face volumes with signs set by outward orientation.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: The one-line formula nabla_a T^a = (1/sqrt(-g)) d_a(sqrt(-g) T^a) is implied but never isolated or illustrated.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Learners miss the most practical consequence of the section.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Derive the polar and spherical coordinate divergence from it as a quick check.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Printed typos in the geodesic derivation: the first line of the left-side evaluation has d/dx for d/du, and the right-side first line shows xdot^x for xdot^b; also the integration-by-parts line in §7.5 has dL/dy in the boundary bracket where dL/dy' is meant.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Careful readers stall trying to make sense of mismatched variables.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Flag the corrections alongside the derivation.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: The Lagrangian is called a functional of y, y' and x, though it is an ordinary function of those variables; only the action is a functional.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Blurs the distinction the section has just defined.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Say L is a function; I is the functional.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Constancy of K along geodesics is asserted rather than derived, and the null-geodesic argument is omitted.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: The recipe feels like magic; learners do not see that K conservation is the first integral from the absence of explicit u-dependence, nor why the same recipe covers light rays.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Show d/du of K along solutions vanishes using the Euler-Lagrange equations (Beltrami-type identity), and note that K never needs division by L.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Killing vectors are not connected to conserved quantities along geodesics (g_ab X^a xdot^b constant) in this chapter.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Symmetry and the K method appear unrelated even though cyclic coordinates in K are exactly Killing directions; the link is only exploited implicitly in Chapter 16.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Add the one-line proof that X_a xdot^a is constant along an affinely parametrized geodesic and illustrate with energy and angular momentum.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: §7.7 opens with coordinate transformations that leave a metric invariant and calls (7.53) an infinitesimal coordinate transformation, while the actual construction is active.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Reinforces the confusion between general covariance (every metric is invariant in form under relabelling) and true symmetries.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Consistently use active language and point out that any metric looks the same after a relabelling but only special metrics have isometries.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: The claim that finite isometries follow from infinitesimal ones glosses over discrete symmetries, completeness of flows and the group structure; the maximum number n(n+1)/2 of Killing vectors is never stated.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Learners may think reflections come from Killing vectors or be surprised by the counts in Exercises 7.11 and 8.5.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: State the exponentiation idea with a picture of integral curves and quote the n(n+1)/2 bound with flat space as the saturating case.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Exercises 7.8 onward are all keyed to §7.7 although 7.8 uses the §7.6 K-Lagrangian.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Minor: a learner filtering exercises by section misses the one practice problem for the K method.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Re-key Exercise 7.8 to §7.6 in any adapted material.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: No figures other than a blob for the divergence theorem, and no worked examples with concrete metrics.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: All three toolkits remain abstract until much later chapters.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Pair each tool with one concrete case: polar-coordinate divergence, geodesics on the 2-sphere via K, Killing vectors of the 2-sphere.

tutor_notes: Open with a quick diagnostic: 'In polar coordinates, why is the area element r dr dtheta and not dr dtheta?' The answer leads straight to densities and sqrt(g).

Teach the three threads separately and signpost the switch: (1) densities and integration, (2) variational method and geodesics, (3) symmetry and Killing vectors. Learners often assume they are one argument.
For densities, start from weights rather than definitions: 'd^4x is weight -1, sqrt(-g) is weight +1, their product is a scalar.' Only then show (7.1) and (7.2).
Check understanding with: 'Is the ordinary divergence d_a V^a of a vector field a scalar?' Expected answer: no in general; yes for sqrt(-g) V^a, giving (1/sqrt(-g)) d_a(sqrt(-g) V^a).
When deriving (7.9), let the learner try a 2x2 matrix by hand first: d(ad - bc) with respect to a is d, the cofactor.
For the Euler-Lagrange derivation, emphasize the two places the endpoint condition is used: killing the boundary term and allowing arbitrary localized bumps in the lemma.

Before introducing K, ask: 'The square-root Lagrangian gives the same action for any parametrization; what does that imply about its Euler-Lagrange equations?' Answer: they cannot determine the parameter, hence the (sddot/sdot) term.

Practise the K method on the 2-sphere (K = (1/2)(thetadot^2 + sin^2 theta phidot^2)): the learner should get Gamma^theta_{phi phi} = -sin theta cos theta and Gamma^phi_{theta phi} = cot theta, watching for the factor of 2 on the mixed term.
Point out that if the metric does not depend on a coordinate, the corresponding momentum dK/dxdot is conserved; this previews Killing vectors and Chapter 16 orbits.

For §7.7, draw the distinction: a relabelling of coordinates changes every metric's components but not the geometry; an isometry is a motion of points that leaves the geometry looking the same. Ask the learner to classify a rotation of the plane and a stretch of the plane.

Good checks: 'Why is d/dx a Killing vector of the Euclidean plane?' (components constant, Lie derivative vanishes); 'Is r d/dr?' (no, it rescales distances). The bracket of d/dx with the rotation -y d/dx + x d/dy is d/dy, as in Exercise 7.13.

Common learner questions: why sqrt(-g) and not sqrt(g) (signature); why not just use d^4x in Cartesian coordinates (curved spacetime has no global Cartesian chart); whether the K-Lagrangian is 'kinetic energy' (formally yes, Chapter 8 makes the link); whether Killing vectors must be timelike (no, rotations are spacelike).
